column1: # THE SAILS. One row per sail a captain can buy.
# Edit here, then: npm run import && npm run catalogue
# A sail belongs to ONE category and fits a berth of that category. That is the whole fitting rule.
# Area is not the category: a topgallant is nearly four times a skysail and both are SSQ.
#   LSQ  Large square    courses, lower topsails            driving power, low on the mast
#   SSQ  Small square    topgallants, royals, skysails,     light-air lift, high up
#   TRI  Headsail        jibs, flying jibs, staysails       set on a stay forward: balance, pointing
#   LAT  Lateen          lateen yards, Bermuda mainsails    triangular canvas driving from a mast
#   GAF  Gaff            gaff mainsails, spankers,          fore-and-aft drive aft, manoeuvre
#   LUG  Lugsail         dipping and standing lug,          the main drive of a lugger
#   STU  Studdingsail    boomed-out extensions             ADDITIVE. Not a berth: see below.
# A LATEEN IS NOT A HEADSAIL. Both are triangles and they were one category until the bowsprit became
# a station: the moment a jib had a berth of its own a lateen fitted it and pulled better, so the
# choice made itself. They do different work, so they are different categories.
# STU does not go in a berth. A studdingsail booms out beyond a square sail that is already set and
# its area comes off that sail, so it is an attachment rather than a place in the rig. Nothing models
# that yet and `npm run catalogue` refuses a berth that asks for one, deliberately, so that a mast
# cannot pretend to carry studdingsails in a slot.
# kind    one of the seven labels above.
# drive   what she pulls, as a share of a course's, which is why a course is exactly 1. Physical area
#         is where this number starts and the proportions are: course 1.00, lower topsail 0.70,
#         topgallant 0.40, royal 0.22, skysail 0.12, studdingsail 0.50 to 0.80 of the square sail it
#         booms out from. Better cloth holds its shape and adds to it, which is why two sails of one
# hand    what it does to her helm. Square canvas stiffens her, so it is negative; fore-and-aft
#         canvas helps her round, so it is positive.
# blurb   one line a captain reads.
# Two grades of most of them: the plain one a captain can afford early, and a fine one in heavier
# cloth that is strictly better and priced for it. Prices are placed against each other and have not
# been tuned against what a voyage actually pays.

column7: blurb
The big lower sail. Plain flax, and it pulls.
The same sail in heavier cloth. Holds its shape when the plain one is bellying out of it.
The sail over the course, and the one she works hardest. Seven tenths of the cloth below it.
A topsail worth setting in weather that would split the plain one.
Third sail up, where the wind is cleaner and every hand aboard is a long way from the deck.
Heavy cloth where it is worth having. She carries it later into a blow.
A small sail over the topgallant, for a captain in a hurry and a sea that will allow it.
The royal a ship keeps set after the plain one would have come in.
A handkerchief in the clouds. It pulls very little and it looks magnificent.
Slung under the bowsprit on a yard athwart. Old fashioned, and it drags her head round.
A small triangle set on a stay. Not much pull, and she feels it in the rudder.
The staysail a captain keeps when she changes ships.
Set out on the bowsprit. What balances her head against everything she carries aft.
Cut flat rather than full, so it holds an edge to the wind the plain one spills.
Right out at the boom end. The last scrap of canvas anybody sets forward.
A long triangle on a raking yard. Less pull than a course, and she comes round on it.
Cut flat rather than full. A xebec runs down what she pleases under one of these.
One tall triangle and no yard at all. Points closer to the wind than square canvas can.
The sail a sloop is really for. She will weather anything of her own size.
Four sided, on a gaff abaft the mast. Handy, and one watch can take it in.
The same sail in cloth that keeps its shape on a long board.
A scrap above the gaff, filling the space nothing else reaches.
The fore-and-aft sail on her after mast. She steers on it as much as on the rudder.
A spanker worth keeping set when the square canvas has come in.
Small, heavy, and bent to a little mast of its own. What she wears when it is blowing.
Four sided on a slung yard, and the yard comes round the mast on every tack.
The lug that stays where it is put. Slower than a dipping lug and far less work.
The sail a Channel lugger shows a revenue cutter her heels under.
A small lug over the mainsail, set flying in light airs.
